outcomes.original: Filing step: Form the legal entity with the California Secretary of State and obtain an EIN from the IRS. What to say: File LLC Articles of Organization (LLC-1) or corporation articles with the California Secretary of State online; the fee is $70 for an LLC or $100 for a corporation. File the Statement of Information within 90 days ($20 for an LLC, due every two years). Then apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS online; it is issued immediately and free. The EIN and entity name are needed for every other permit, the bank account, the lease and the liquor licence.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register for a California seller's permit with CDTFA and a San Francisco business registration certificate with the Treasurer & Tax Collector. What to say: Register online with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) for a seller's permit; it is free and often issued the same day. ABC will not issue a liquor licence until the seller's permit exists, so do this early. Then register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector within 30 days of starting business in the city; the fee is tiered by gross receipts (e.g. $55 up to $100k, $625 at $1–1.5M for 2026–27). Every other city department asks for the Business Account Number (BAN), so register immediately after forming the entity.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File a fictitious business name (DBA) statement with the County Clerk if the public-facing name differs from the legal entity name. What to say: File the FBN statement with the San Francisco County Clerk in person (photo ID) or by mail, then publish in a court-approved newspaper once a week for four weeks and file proof of publication within 45 days. The total cost is about $60–120. Banks and ABC want the filed statement. If the restaurant name matches the legal entity name exactly, skip this step.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit DPH plan check for the kitchen build-out at the same time as the building permit application to DBI. What to say: Any new food facility or remodel affecting the kitchen needs DPH approval of plans, finishes, equipment and menu. Submit two sets of scaled drawings, interior/exterior photos and a menu through the DPH portal; the 2026–27 flat fee is $2,207 for a new restaurant (8 hours), with extra review at $276/hr. DBI will route the building permit application to DPH for plan check; coordinate with your architect to submit both applications at the same time. After approval, schedule a pre-final inspection at ~80% complete and a final inspection, booking each with your plan reviewer at least two weeks ahead.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the building permit application with DBI for tenant improvements, including kitchen build-out, hood, grease interceptor, plumbing, electrical and ADA upgrades. What to say: Submit stamped architectural plans with a complete scope of work (kitchen, hood, grease interceptor, restrooms, ADA upgrades) to DBI. Fees are a percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–15,000. The application is routed to Planning for zoning review (Section 175), DPH for health plan check, SFPUC for grease interceptor review, and SFFD for hood suppression system review. Separate electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are pulled by licensed subcontractors. Hire an architect who has done San Francisco restaurants; incomplete plan sets bounce between departments and add months. Do not start construction before the permit is issued.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Install a grease interceptor and submit the Installation Verification Form to SFPUC under the Fats, Oils & Grease (FOG) program. What to say: Under the FOG Control Ordinance every food service establishment that cooks must install grease-capturing equipment; SFPUC inspectors assign a Discharger Category (1–3) that dictates the device type, and new restaurants must install it before opening. Submitting the Installation Verification Form earns a 14.2% reduction on the sewer portion of your bill. An undersized or missing interceptor is a common reason DBI withholds final sign-off. Coordinate with your plumber and the building permit review.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Schedule Fire Department inspections for the commercial kitchen hood and place of assembly (if occupant load is 50 or more). What to say: Commercial cooking hoods need a suppression-system plan review and inspection routed with the building permit. If the occupant load is 50 or more, obtain a Place of Assembly permit from the SFFD Bureau of Fire Prevention ($446, 49 South Van Ness Suite 560) and a posted occupancy sign. The Entertainment Commission also requires this permit for venues of 50+. Schedule the final fire inspection before the DPH pre-opening inspection, typically two weeks ahead.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for the ABC Type 41 licence after DPH plan check is approved and the building permit is issued. What to say: File the Type 41 application online with ABC, attaching the signed lease, seller's permit, zoning sign-off from Planning (the ABC referral approval), and the entity documents. The initial fee is about $1,000–1,600. Post the public notice at the premises for 30 days. ABC sends the application to the Police Department and Planning Department for review; expect 60–120 days if unprotested. If the census tract is over its authorised count and ABC flags undue concentration, start the Public Convenience or Necessity (PCN) letter request from Planning at the same time you apply to ABC; recent approvals in this corridor show no PCN delays, but confirm with ABC's district office or Planning's ABC liaison before filing.
outcomes.note: Record does not specify filing must be after DPH/building permit, online filing method, entity documents, specific review agencies, corridor history, or liaison confirmation advice.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for the health permit to operate at least one month before opening, after DPH plan check is approved and one certified food safety manager is on staff. What to say: Apply online with your BAN, Location ID (LIN) and federal tax ID; the $470 permit to operate application (2026–27) includes the initial inspection. The 2026–27 annual licence fee for restaurants and bars is $0 for 2026–28; reinspections are $276/hr. A change of ownership or entity type needs a new permit, and you cannot serve the public before it is issued. Walk the space against the DPH checklist a week before the inspection: missing hand sinks, unsealed surfaces or no hot water are the most common reasons for failed pre-opening inspections, which push openings by 2–3 weeks.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 14 to 45 days. Estimated government cost: $470 to $1,000. Notes: The time and cost shown are for the one approval the rules could decide: the health permit to operate. The health permit is issued 14–45 days after plan check and inspection, at a cost of $470–1,000 in government fees (2026–27 schedule). This is a time to approval, not to a denial or a withdrawal. The rules set the zoning, alcohol and building rows to insufficient information, so no timeline or cost is given for those approvals until the missing inputs are confirmed. Once the applicant confirms whether the business is a chain, the square footage, how the liquor licence will be obtained, what the space was last used as, the occupant load, and the existing occupancy group, the rules can decide whether a conditional use authorization, an ABC Type 41 licence investigation, or a building permit with change of occupancy applies. If the use is principally permitted (non-chain, under 2,500 square feet, first story) and the space was last used as a restaurant with no change of occupancy, expect the ABC Type 41 to take 60–120 days and the building permit 14–120 days, with combined government fees of roughly $3,000–18,000 depending on construction valuation. If a conditional use authorization is required (formula retail or over 2,500 square feet), add 120–300 days and $3,100–15,000 for the Planning Commission hearing.
